target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove work/school scheduling barriers at the source by giving people time off to vote.
objection: Declaring Election Day a federal holiday does not generally require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many hourly retail and service workers—especially low-income workers—would still have to work or would lose wages if they voted. Because the holiday label alone would not reliably free these voters' time, it would not be a dependable turnout strategy and could disadvantage the workers least able to absorb unpaid leave.

target: AG2's objection that a national holiday is only a label private employers can ignore, so it would not meaningfully change schedules.
objection: A national holiday can be implemented through law in a way that guarantees voters time to vote, such as job-protected time off, a required voting window, and school-calendar adjustments. Under that kind of implementation, workers are not left with the same work-day constraint, so the policy can directly reduce scheduling barriers rather than merely shifting them.

target: AG1's response that a holiday plus implementation details would solve the access problem, and that holiday status itself directly reduces barriers.
objection: The claimed barrier reduction does not come from the holiday label itself. If access is ensured by separate job-protected time-off rules or school-calendar changes, then those enforceable protections are doing the work, while the holiday designation alone does not reliably remove the work/school barrier for low-income workers.

target: AG2's claim that because a holiday does not automatically mandate employer closure or paid leave, it will not reliably give people time to vote.
objection: That conclusion does not follow. In practice, national holidays change observed scheduling: schools close or run modified calendars, and many employers voluntarily adjust shifts, hours, or staffing around major holidays. So holiday status can reduce the work/school reporting requirement for a substantial share of voters, even without separate voting-window legislation.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday itself will directly reduce scheduling barriers for many voters.
objection: A federal holiday does not, by itself, require private employers to close or provide paid time off. Many low-income retail and service workers would still be scheduled to work, and the lost-wage or unpaid-time burden would remain. Any real barrier reduction would require additional enforceable labor protections, not merely holiday status.

target: AG2's argument that holiday designation alone does not reliably give people time off because it does not legally force private workplaces to close.
objection: That assumption is too narrow. Even without a separate voting-window statute, a national holiday changes real-world scheduling because schools typically close and many employers follow holiday calendars by reducing hours, closing locations, or using holiday pay. That makes the day more available for voting and removes a substantial portion of the work/school constraint.

target: AG1's broader claim that holiday status is an effective way to increase turnout by reducing scheduling pressure.
objection: Research and experience indicate that election-day holidays alone are not a strong turnout reform. The more effective measures are direct access reforms such as enforceable voting-time protections, expanded early or absentee voting, easier registration, and reduced wait times. So the holiday designation by itself is not a substantively reliable turnout strategy.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday cannot reliably reduce barriers because schools and workplaces may still operate normally.
objection: That underestimates the practical effect of changing the calendar. Making Election Day a national holiday would directly remove a major source of the barrier—the need to be in school or at work on Election Day—because many schools and workplaces do in fact treat federal holidays differently. The holiday therefore can remove the core scheduling constraint for many voters.

target: AG1's later claim that a holiday can protect workers from income loss even if they still need time off to vote.
objection: A national holiday does not necessarily provide paid time off or wage replacement. Workers could still be required to take unpaid leave or have hours cut, which means low-income hourly workers still face the income-loss barrier unless the policy separately guarantees pay.

target: AG2's point that workers might still lose wages unless wage replacement is separately guaranteed.
objection: The main barrier is being scheduled to work or attend school on Election Day. A national holiday changes the calendar so that many workplaces and schools are not operating normally, giving people time to vote without necessarily losing wages. Even if some workers still must work, the holiday can still provide accessible time off for many voters.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday changes calendars and time structure in a way that gives workers real time off.
objection: Federal holiday designation generally affects observance, but it does not compel private employers to close or provide paid time off. Many hourly retail and service workers would still work on that day, so the supposed time-off benefit depends on additional labor protections rather than on the holiday label itself.

target: AG2's claim that wage loss would still block workers unless paid leave is separately mandated.
objection: A national holiday can be enacted through legislation that includes job-protected voting time and prevents wage penalties, such as paid time to vote or wage replacement. If those protections are part of the holiday statute, low-income workers are not forced into unpaid leave, and the holiday itself becomes the mechanism that protects their pay while enabling voting.

target: AG1's argument that job-protected time off or voting windows bundled with a holiday mean low-income workers are no longer blocked.
objection: If the barrier is removed by separately enforceable job-protected or wage-protection rules, then the reduction comes from those labor provisions, not from making Election Day a holiday. Without explicit wage replacement or strong enforcement, workers can still be forced into unpaid time or reduced hours, which low-income workers cannot absorb.

target: AG2's implication that a national holiday cannot include enforceable wage protection and therefore cannot avoid unpaid leave for workers.
objection: A national holiday is created by law and can include enforceable requirements such as paid time to vote or wage replacement. If Election Day is made a holiday through legislation that also prohibits wage penalties, hourly workers are not forced into unpaid leave, so the holiday can itself be the legal package that protects workers' pay.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday is the most appropriate way to increase turnout because it addresses day-of scheduling barriers.
objection: Turnout is constrained by more than whether Election Day is a day off. Many voters face pre-Election-Day problems such as registration and administrative friction, which a holiday does nothing to fix. Automatic voter registration and state employer-time-off rules are more targeted responses than a national holiday.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is not the most reliable turnout strategy because it leaves registration problems untouched.
objection: The holiday is meant to address a different, real day-of barrier: many eligible voters cannot vote because they are scheduled to work or attend school on Election Day. It is reasonable to combine a holiday with other reforms, so the fact that other barriers exist does not make the holiday ineffective or a reason to reject it.

target: AG1's assumption that a federal holiday gives workers actual time off from private-sector jobs.
objection: Federal holiday status generally does not require private employers to provide paid time off or stop scheduling work. Many hourly retail and service workers would still be required to work, so the work/school timing conflict persists unless additional job-protected or paid voting-time rules are enacted.

target: AG2's argument that pre-election barriers and other reforms make a holiday ineffective.
objection: Pre-Election-Day barriers do not negate the value of a holiday, because the holiday addresses a separate day-of constraint. For many eligible voters, the key problem is that work or school makes voting impractical on Election Day. A national holiday directly removes that obstacle and can work alongside other reforms.

target: AG1's underlying assumption that calling Election Day a national holiday reliably removes the day-of scheduling constraint for voters.
objection: That assumption is false as a general matter. Federal holiday designation usually affects observance, not private employers' staffing or paid leave policies, so many hourly workers can still be scheduled to work and may have to take unpaid time or lose wages. The scheduling barrier is not reliably removed by the holiday label alone.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday should be rejected because it does not solve registration and other pre-election barriers.
objection: A holiday targets a different, concrete barrier: people being required to be at work or school on Election Day. It also frames voting as a civic celebration, which can increase the salience of participation and strengthen motivation. So the holiday is justified by both barrier removal and symbolic encouragement, even if other reforms are also needed.

target: AG1's claim that holiday symbolism and day-of scheduling effects are enough to boost turnout.
objection: Research suggests election-day holidays alone are not an effective way to increase participation. Any turnout gains tend to come from additional, enforceable access reforms—such as guaranteed time off with wage protection, expanded absentee or early voting, and reduced administrative barriers—rather than from the holiday status or symbolic celebration framing.

target: AG2's suggestion that a national holiday is not a dependable way to improve access for work/school-constrained voters.
objection: For many voters, the decisive barrier is simply being scheduled to work or attend school on Election Day. Moving Election Day to a non-working day directly changes that schedule and is a workable approach in many democracies, as reflected by broad domestic support and the fact that many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays.

target: AG1's assumption that a federal holiday reliably gives private-sector workers time away from work with no wage penalty.
objection: Federal holiday status usually does not compel private employers to close or provide paid leave. Many hourly retail and service workers—especially low-income workers—can still be scheduled to work and may have to absorb lost wages if they vote, so the supposed time-off benefit is not broadly reliable.

target: AG2's view that pre-election barriers mean a holiday should not be adopted.
objection: The existence of pre-election barriers is not a reason to reject a holiday that directly reduces a major day-of obstacle. For eligible voters who are already in the system, the school/work schedule is what makes voting impractical or impossible on Election Day, and a holiday changes that calendar constraint.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday reliably removes the school/work constraint that blocks voting.
objection: A holiday label does not generally control private employers' staffing or paid-leave policies. Many hourly workers can still be required to work on Election Day, leaving the practical constraint intact unless separate job-protected time or wage-replacement rules are enacted.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday should not be adopted because other barriers also matter.
objection: Even if other barriers exist, a national holiday still removes a real, major day-of obstacle for many eligible voters who are scheduled to work or attend school. It reduces an important barrier rather than leaving the core problem untouched, and it can be paired with other reforms.

target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday reliably increases turnout by removing day-of scheduling barriers.
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically require private employers to close or provide paid leave. Many hourly retail and service workers can still be scheduled to work and may have to take unpaid time or suffer wage losses, so the day-of scheduling barrier often remains even after the holiday is declared.

target: AG2's view that because other barriers exist, a holiday is not substantively warranted.
objection: The holiday addresses a specific and important barrier: the fact that many voters are scheduled to work or attend school on Election Day. Since turnout is influenced by multiple constraints, removing this one directly is still valuable, and other reforms can complement it.

target: AG1's repeated claim that a national holiday itself reliably eliminates work/school scheduling barriers.
objection: That claim is not generally true. In the U.S., federal holiday status usually affects observance rather than private employers' closure or paid-leave policies, so many hourly retail and service workers remain scheduled to work or face unpaid time. Barrier relief depends on additional enforceable protections, not on the holiday label alone.
